endorsements.title: Considerations for the regulation of generative AI-enabled medical devices (discussion paper)
endorsements.quote: Relevant testing may include multi-turn simulated encounters that assess time to escalation in evolving presentations, the quality of escalation language and handoff information, and resistance to over-reassurance when users minimize symptoms or resist escalation.

endorsements.title: Reasoning in Real World Clinical Care: Why Large Language Models Are Not Yet Safe for Autonomous Clinical Decision Support
endorsements.quote: A safe-triage evaluation must instead reward the behaviors the preceding sections showed to be missing: widening under uncertainty, lowering the threshold for escalation, deferring when information is insufficient, and resisting minimized or adversarial histories.

endorsements.title: It Is the Journey, Not the Destination: Moving From End Points to Trajectories When Assessing Chatbot Mental Health Safety
endorsements.quote: It is important that baseline vulnerable phenotypes (such as the aforementioned forms of vulnerability and additional phenotypes including neurodivergence, eating disorders, and body dysmorphia) are taken into consideration when assessing potential mental health risks and likelihood of epistemic drift, although there should also be scope for assessing risk trajectories in interactions where, at baseline, there is no apparent psychological vulnerability.

endorsements.title: Responsible artificial intelligence integration framework for psychiatric guidelines
endorsements.quote: Red-team exercises must simulate high-risk, ethically ambiguous, and culturally sensitive scenarios, with documented review of system responses and escalation pathways.

evidence.title: Conversational multi-turn interaction does not ensure triage-disposition alignment in ChatGPT Health in real and synthetic patient encounters
evidence.outcome: Whether multi-turn simulated nurse-style questioning improved triage-disposition agreement versus single-turn
evidence.effect: Multi-turn 55.7% vs single-turn 52.9% agreement against nurse line standards; clinician-adjudicated agreement 48.2% multi-turn vs 54.1% single-turn; no consistent improvement.
evidence.quote: These findings suggest conversational interaction does not ensure safe triage-disposition alignment.
evidence.sample_unit: cases (vignettes, emergency department cases, nurse line cases)

evidence.title: "AI Psychosis" in Context: How Conversation History Shapes LLM Responses to Delusional Beliefs
evidence.outcome: Model validation of delusional beliefs versus challenge and referral across increasing conversation context
evidence.effect: Unsafe-tier models validated or elaborated delusional premises and attempted harm reduction inside the delusional frame; safer models challenged beliefs and directed the user to external support, using the established relationship.
evidence.quote: Safer models, however, often used the established relationship to support intervention, challenging delusional beliefs and directing the user to external support.
evidence.sample_unit: LLMs tested across three levels of accumulated context

evidence.title: LLMs for Medical Consultation Are Evaluated Too Late: The Preformulation Gap
evidence.outcome: Self-care advice given before any patient answer in multi-turn vignettes with vague or minimized concerns
evidence.effect: Self-care or home-management advice before any patient answer appeared in 9 of 12 baseline case-model cells and 0 of 12 instruction cells.
evidence.quote: Self-care or home-management advice before any patient answer appeared in 9 of 12 baseline case-model cells and 0 of 12 instruction cells, while structured handoff summaries appeared in 0 of 12 and 10 of 12 cells, respectively.

evidence.title: AI-Powered Triage of Suicidal Ideation in Adolescents: A Comparative Evaluation of Large Language Models Using Synthetic Clinical Vignettes
evidence.outcome: Inappropriate therapeutic reassurance in triage action plans
evidence.effect: Models generated clinically inappropriate therapeutic reassurance in a triage context, among pervasive critical failures.
evidence.quote: However, significant and critical failures were pervasive, including the omission of crucial inquiries about access to lethal means, failure to incorporate protective factors into planning, and the generation of clinically inappropriate therapeutic reassurance in a triage context.

evidence.title: ChatGPT Health performance in a structured test of triage recommendations
evidence.outcome: Triage shift when family or friends minimized symptoms (anchoring)
evidence.effect: Triage recommendations shifted significantly in edge cases (OR = 11.7, 95% CI 3.7-36.6), with most shifts toward less urgent care.
evidence.quote: When family or friends minimized symptoms, indicating anchoring bias, triage recommendations shifted significantly in edge cases (odds ratio = 11.7, 95% confidence interval = 3.7-36.6), with the majority of shifts toward less urgent care.

evidence.title: The Psychogenic Machine: Simulating AI Psychosis, Delusion Reinforcement and Harm Enablement in Large Language Models
evidence.outcome: Delusion confirmation and safety intervention across evolving multi-turn simulated conversations, explicit versus implicit
evidence.effect: Mean DCS 0.91 ± 0.88; implicit scenarios had more delusion confirmation, more harm enablement, and fewer interventions (p < .001).
evidence.quote: Performance was significantly worse in implicit scenarios, models were more likely to confirm delusions and enable harm while offering fewer interventions (p < .001).

evidence.title: MedPRESS: A Multi-turn Benchmark for Patient-Pressure-Induced Medical Sycophancy in LLMs
evidence.outcome: Model shift to unsafe agreement under escalating patient pressure in five-turn dialogues, including symptom triage and care resistance
evidence.effect: Models frequently shift toward unsafe agreement under repeated patient pressure, varying by family, scale and prompt type; anti-sycophancy prompting improves several models but does not eliminate unsafe agreement.
evidence.quote: Results show that models frequently shift toward unsafe agreement under repeated patient pressure, with substantial variation across model families, model scale, and prompt type.

evidence.title: When Vocabulary Comprehension Fails Clinical Reasoning: Evaluating Therapy Bots' Safety Risks for Generation Alpha
evidence.outcome: Acceptance of symptom minimization by AI across conversation turns
evidence.effect: Minimization acceptance failure pattern produced a 43pp gap, the largest of six identified failure patterns.
evidence.quote: We identify six failure patterns: sarcasm masking (29pp), minimization acceptance (43pp), informal style bias (24pp), risk-stratified ambiguity (19pp), semantic drift (19pp), context-dependent violence (7pp).

evidence.title: Reasoning Before Disposition: A Model-Agnostic Cannot-Miss Discipline for Quiet Emergencies and the Case for Deterministic Enforcement
evidence.outcome: Sensitivity for overt emergencies when patient minimizes or denies symptoms or third party reassures
evidence.effect: Across 40 unambiguous emergencies in five framings on Opus 4.8, sensitivity stayed at or above 97.5% in every arm and was flat across framings.
evidence.quote: sensitivity stayed at or above 97.5% in every arm and was flat across framings
evidence.sample_unit: emergency vignette stems (subtle or atypical emergencies)

commentary.bottom_line: One simulated study compared multi-turn with single-turn questioning and found no consistent gain in triage agreement, and no study tested whether multi-turn evaluation detects over-reassurance or poor handoffs before deployment. Eight hazard studies show that models often accept symptom minimization or shift toward less urgent advice under pressure, which supports the concern the recommendation targets.

perspectives.view: The one study near the practice asked whether multi-turn questioning changes model triage, and it did not ask whether multi-turn evaluation finds failures. Agreement was 55.7% multi-turn versus 52.9% single-turn against nurse line standards, and 48.2% versus 54.1% on clinician adjudication. A single indirect, inconsistent, level 4 simulated study supports a very low certainty rating.

The hazard studies suggest the failure appears across turns and under social pressure. Triage shifted in edge cases when family or friends minimized symptoms (OR = 11.7, 95% CI 3.7-36.6), mostly toward less urgent care, and minimization acceptance showed a 43pp gap. Sensitivity for unambiguous emergencies stayed at or above 97.5% across framings, so subtle cases may need this testing most.

Multi-turn simulation appears feasible in benchmark form, with one benchmark running 600 five-turn dialogues and another running 1536 simulated turns. Results varied by model family, scale, and prompt type, and implicit scenarios produced more delusion confirmation and fewer interventions than explicit ones (p < .001). Test sets may need implicit and pressured presentations to separate safer from less safe models.

The regulatory discussion paper says this testing may be included, and the two commentaries say it should occur, but none supplies pass thresholds, scenario sets, or outcome data. Because the only direct study is simulated and retrospective, adopting this as an expectation would set an evaluation standard before evidence shows it predicts real-world escalation performance.

The emergency sensitivity benchmark was the only study with limited English proficiency content, and it tested overt emergencies rather than the practice. The direct test did not report Medicaid, safety-net, or literacy characteristics. Symptom minimization and resistance to care may be expressed differently across languages and cultures, so scenario sets built without these groups may miss failures that affect them.

Self-care advice before any patient answer appeared in 9 of 12 baseline cells and 0 of 12 instruction cells in one vignette study. In a pressure benchmark, anti-sycophancy prompting reduced but did not eliminate unsafe agreement. For patients who downplay symptoms, these results suggest a chatbot may withhold a route to a human unless testing checks for it.

commentary.research_gap: No study has tested whether multi-turn escalation testing before deployment identifies models that later over-reassure real users, and no study measured the quality of escalation language or handoff information. Prospective studies should compare models that pass or fail such testing on real-world escalation outcomes, using scenario sets that include Medicaid, safety-net, limited English proficiency, and low-literacy users.
commentary.underserved_note: The one study testing the practice did not report Medicaid, safety-net, limited English proficiency, or low-literacy populations. Only one hazard study included limited English proficiency content, and it tested emergency sensitivity rather than the practice. The evidence therefore cannot show whether multi-turn escalation testing works for these groups, who may express minimization in ways current scenario sets do not capture.
